title: National vaccination booking
tagline: Let millions of invited residents grab a limited set of appointment slots without overbooking or melting down.
govtech_note: OGP built the booking system Singapore used for COVID-19 vaccination appointments. The publicly visible shape: residents were invited in waves by age group, got an SMS with a personal booking link, and many tried to book in the first minutes after each wave opened. Treat this as domain-flavoured practice: there is no evidence GovTech asks it as an interview question, and the design below is a reasonable one, not a description of the real system. It is a strong vehicle for the topics interviewers do probe: contention, correctness under concurrency, and graceful overload.
summary: The hard part is not storage (a few GB) but contention. Hundreds of thousands of people arrive in the same minute and fight over a few thousand popular slots. The design has three ideas: a waiting room that admits people at a rate the backend can serve, a reserve-then-confirm flow where a slot is held for 5 minutes, and an atomic conditional UPDATE plus unique constraints so that no slot is ever overbooked and no person is ever booked twice, even when code has bugs or requests are retried.

functional: Invite residents in waves (by age group) with a personal SMS link
Browse centres and see roughly how many slots remain per time window
Hold a slot (or a dose 1 + dose 2 pair) for a few minutes, then confirm
Reschedule or cancel; the freed slot goes back into the pool
Send a confirmation SMS and a reminder the day before
nonfunctional: Never overbook a slot and never give one person two active bookings for the same dose
Survive a launch spike of ~2k arrivals/s without errors; queue people instead of failing them
Fair: people who arrive earlier are served earlier; bots and shared links get no edge
Confirmed bookings are durable (strong consistency on the booking write path)
Availability counts may be a few seconds stale
out_of_scope: Clinical records and dose administration at the centre
Centre staffing and vaccine stock logistics

estimates.label: Launch rush
estimates.calc: 1M invited in a wave, 30% open the link in the first 10 min → 300k ÷ 600 s

estimates.label: Admit rate
estimates.calc: ~10 API calls per booking; API sized for ~3k req/s → 3,000 ÷ 10

estimates.label: Wait for the last of the rush

api.desc: Waiting room. Returns your position, or a signed pass (10 min) once admitted.
Pass required. Checks the single-use invite and identity; returns eligibility.
Remaining slots per window. Served from cache, may be ~2 s stale.
Atomically takes 1 or 2 slots. 201 {holdId, expiresAt}; 409 if any slot is full or you already hold one.
Turns a live hold into bookings. 201; 410 if the hold expired. Retries return the same booking.
Reschedule: take the new slot and free the old one in one transaction.
Cancel; the slot returns to the pool.

data.name: slots
data.note: taken counts live holds plus bookings. The CHECK constraint makes overbooking impossible even if application code is wrong.

data.name: holds
data.note: One live hold per person. Expired rows are deleted by the sweeper, which gives the seats back.

data.name: bookings
data.note: Partial unique index on (resident_id, dose_no) WHERE status = 'active': nobody gets two active dose-1 bookings.

data.name: invites
data.note: Store a hash of the link token, never the token itself, so a DB leak cannot be replayed.

data.name: avail:{centre}:{date}
data.note: Read-only view for browsing. Never used to decide who gets a slot.

data.name: waiting room
data.note: Your ticket number is your arrival order; the pointer moves forward at the admit rate.

flows.name: Launch rush: get in and hold a slot

steps.note: At 10:00 a wave of 1M invites becomes valid and ~500 people/s tap their link. Every request lands on the waiting room first, which is cheap: a static page plus one Redis INCR to hand out a ticket number.

The admit pointer advances at ~300 tickets/s, the rate the booking path can sustain. Ticket 120,000 waits about 120,000 ÷ 300 = ~7 min, and the page tells them so. Queueing people is better than letting the API return 503s that make everyone hit refresh.
Admitted users get a signed pass (short-lived token, 10 min). The API checks the signature locally with no DB call, so requests without a pass are rejected for almost no cost.
Show remaining slots per window from Redis, rebuilt every 2 s. It can be slightly stale, and that is fine: it only guides the choice. The real check happens on the next hop.

Hold: UPDATE slots SET taken = taken + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND taken < capacity. One row updated means you got it; zero rows means it just filled, so suggest the next window. Insert a hold row with expires_at = now() + 5 min in the same transaction.
Return {holdId, expiresAt}. The UI shows a 5-minute countdown. Short holds stop people from sitting on seats they will not use.

flows.name: Confirm and get an SMS
flows.desc: Turning a hold into a booking.

steps.note: Resident presses Confirm. The request carries an Idempotency-Key, because on a slow mobile network people press twice and clients retry.

One transaction: delete the hold WHERE id = $1 AND expires_at > now() (must hit 1 row, else 410 Gone), insert the bookings. The partial unique index on (resident_id, dose_no) rejects a second active booking for the same dose.
After commit, publish a booked event (or write it to an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it, so the event can never be lost if the API crashes between commit and publish).
A worker picks it up. The booking is already safe; the SMS is a convenience, so it is async and can retry for minutes without the user waiting.
Send at the provider's contracted rate (say 200 SMS/s) using a token bucket. On repeated 5xx from the primary, fail over to the second provider.
Confirmation SMS with date, centre and a manage-booking link. Dedupe by booking id so a retried job does not send two texts.

flows.name: Invite a wave and send reminders

steps.note: Invites go out in waves (for example by age group), not all at once. Waves are the first fairness and load-control tool: they shrink the crowd that races for slots at any moment.
Select eligible residents not yet booked, in pages of 10k. Create invite rows with a random 128-bit token; store only its hash.
Enqueue invite jobs. 1M SMS at 200/s takes ~83 min, so the wave's booking window should open after the last SMS is out, or the people texted last are at a disadvantage.
The same workers handle invites, confirmations and the day-before reminders the scheduler queues each evening.
Rate-limit per provider; retry with backoff. Track per-message status so you can resend to failures only.
The link carries the token, e.g. /b/8f3k.... It is single-use for booking and is tied to the invited person's identity check, so forwarding it to a friend does not help them.
About a third of holds are abandoned (people compare options, or their phone dies). Without a sweeper those seats would stay locked forever.
Every 30 s: DELETE FROM holds WHERE expires_at < now() RETURNING slot_ids, then taken = taken - 1 for each, in one transaction so the count never drifts.
Within 2 s the availability view shows the seat again and the next person can take it. Holds of 5 min with a 30 s sweep means a seat is idle at most ~5.5 min.

deep.title: The waiting room
deep.html:
A spike of 2k arrivals/s against a backend that can admit 300/s cannot be solved by autoscaling alone: the database primary is the real limit, and it does not autoscale in seconds. So queue people at the edge.

  • Ticket: INCR arrivals in Redis gives each arrival a number. Store it in a signed cookie so refreshing does not lose your place.
  • Admit pointer: a controller raises admitted_up_to by ~300 every second, and slows down automatically if API p99 latency or DB CPU climbs.
  • Pre-opening crowd: people who arrive before 10:00 are all equally early. Give them a random order at 10:00 instead of rewarding whoever has the fastest script, then FIFO for later arrivals.
  • The waiting room page is static and served from a CDN, so it holds up when nothing else would.

deep.title: Never double book: layers of defence
deep.html:
1. Atomic conditional update on the slot row (WHERE taken < capacity). The check and the write happen in one statement, so two requests can never both see "1 left" and both take it. This replaces read-then-write, which is the classic race.
  2. CHECK (taken <= capacity) as a database-level backstop.
  3. Unique constraints on people: one live hold per resident, one active booking per (resident, dose).
  4. Idempotency keys on confirm, so retries return the first result instead of creating a second booking.

Alternatives: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (pessimistic lock, holds the row lock across a round trip) or a version column with optimistic retry (fine when contention is low, but under a launch rush most attempts fail and retry, which multiplies load). The single conditional UPDATE is simplest and holds the lock for microseconds.

deep.title: Hot slots
deep.html:
Saturday 10:00 at the nearest centre is wanted by thousands at once. Every hold on that slot updates the same row, and Postgres serialises writers on a row lock: at ~1 ms per update you get ~1,000 updates/s on that row at best, and long queues of waiting transactions.

  • Split the counter: store the capacity of 20 as 4 sub-rows of 5 and pick one at random; try another if it is full. Contention drops ~4×.
  • Gate in Redis first: a Lua script decrements remaining atomically; only winners go to Postgres for the durable write, losers get "full" in under 1 ms. Postgres stays the source of truth and a reconciler fixes any drift.
  • Steer demand: show the next 3 nearby windows with space when a slot fills, so retries spread out instead of hammering one row.

deep.title: Two doses and rescheduling
deep.html:
A dose-1 slot is useless without a dose-2 slot about 3 to 4 weeks later, so hold both in one transaction. Lock the two slot rows in a fixed order (lower id first) so two transactions holding the same pair in opposite order cannot deadlock.

Reschedule is take-new then release-old in one transaction. Doing it as cancel then book can leave the person with nothing if the new slot fills in between.

tradeoffs.pick: Postgres rows with expires_at, plus a sweeper
tradeoffs.why: Redis keys with TTL expire neatly, but then the seat count lives in two systems and can drift if a process dies mid-way. Keeping holds and counts in one transactional store is easier to reason about; Redis serves only the browse view.

tradeoffs.choice: Concurrency control on the slot row
tradeoffs.why: Holds the row lock for one statement. Optimistic versioning thrashes under heavy contention; SELECT FOR UPDATE holds the lock across a network round trip.

tradeoffs.choice: Absorb the spike: autoscale or queue?
tradeoffs.pick: Waiting room in front, autoscaled API behind it
tradeoffs.why: The DB primary is the bottleneck and cannot scale in seconds. A waiting room turns errors into a visible wait and keeps the order fair.

tradeoffs.pick: Invite waves + first come, first served within a wave
tradeoffs.why: A ballot is fairer for very scarce slots but needs a second round of notifications. With enough total capacity, waves keep each race small and FCFS is easy to explain.

tradeoffs.choice: Exact or approximate availability on the browse page?
tradeoffs.why: Reads outnumber holds ~10:1. The conditional UPDATE is the real arbiter, so staleness costs at most one "just filled, try 10:30" message.

bottlenecks.issue: One popular slot row becomes a lock hotspot
bottlenecks.fix: Split capacity into sub-rows, gate with an atomic Redis decrement, and suggest nearby windows when a slot fills.

bottlenecks.issue: SMS provider throttles or fails during a 1M-invite wave
bottlenecks.fix: Queue + token bucket per provider, a second provider for failover, and open booking only after the wave's last SMS is sent.

bottlenecks.issue: Bots or forwarded links grab slots
bottlenecks.fix: Single-use invite token bound to an identity check, a pass from the waiting room, per-identity and per-IP rate limits, and one hold per resident.
Serve browsing only from the Redis view rebuilt every 2 s; the database sees only holds and confirms.

followups.q: What happens if the API crashes after taking the slot but before replying?
followups.a: The hold row was committed with taken + 1, so the seat is accounted for. The client retries; since the resident already has a live hold (unique per resident) we return it instead of taking a second seat. If they never come back, the sweeper frees it after 5 minutes.

followups.q: How do you stop a script from booking for many people?
followups.a: Each invite is single-use and tied to one person's identity check, holds are limited to one per resident, and admitted passes are rate-limited per identity and IP. A script gains nothing by being fast because the pre-opening crowd is randomised.

followups.q: How would you add a ballot instead of first come, first served?
followups.a: Collect preferences for a window (say 24 h), then run an allocation job: shuffle applicants with a seeded random order, assign each their highest-ranked preference with space, and notify results in a batch. No real-time contention at all, at the cost of a slower answer.

followups.q: A centre closes for a day. What do you do?
followups.a: Set those slots' capacity to 0, find active bookings on them, and offer each person a one-tap move to the nearest centre with space, holding the new slot for them for 24 h. All of it is a batch job plus notifications; the core schema does not change.

followups.q: Why not just put everything in Redis for speed?
followups.a: Bookings must survive failures and be auditable. Postgres gives transactions, constraints and durable writes at the ~600 txn/s we need. Redis is used where losing data is harmless: the availability view and the waiting-room counters.

quiz.q: Which statement prevents two people taking the last seat?
options: SELECT taken FROM slots, then UPDATE if taken < capacity
UPDATE slots SET taken = taken + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND taken < capacity
Cache the remaining count in Redis with a TTL
Retry the booking until it succeeds
quiz.why: The check and the write are one atomic statement. Read-then-write lets both requests read "1 left" before either writes.

quiz.q: Why do holds have a short expiry?
options: To save disk space
So abandoned sessions give seats back instead of locking them forever
Because SMS links expire
To make the browse page faster
quiz.why: Many holds are abandoned. A 5-minute hold plus a sweeper returns those seats to the pool.

quiz.q: What does the waiting room protect most directly?
options: The CDN
The SMS provider
The database primary, which cannot scale out in seconds
The browser
quiz.why: Stateless API servers autoscale; the single write primary does not. The admit rate is set by what it can handle.

quiz.q: A resident double-taps Confirm on a slow network. What stops two bookings?
options: The CDN cache
An Idempotency-Key plus a unique index on (resident_id, dose_no) for active bookings
The hold sweeper
Rate limiting by IP
quiz.why: The retry returns the first result, and even a buggy client cannot create a second active booking for the same dose.

quiz.q: Two transactions each hold a dose-1 and dose-2 slot pair in opposite order. How do you avoid deadlock?
options: Lock rows in a fixed order, such as by slot id
Use a bigger connection pool
Set a longer lock timeout
Hold the slots in two separate transactions
quiz.why: A consistent lock order removes the cycle that causes deadlock. Separate transactions would let someone end up with dose 1 but no dose 2.
